summary: This informational memo describes the Host Identity namespace, a cryptographic namespace for applications, and the Host Identity Protocol layer between internetworking and transport layers. It supports end-host mobility, multihoming and NAT traversal. It obsoletes RFC 4423 and addresses concerns raised by the IESG, including crypto agility.

eli5.summary: Normally a computer is known by where it sits. This document describes a way to name computers by a secret-based identity instead, so a laptop can move around and still be recognized.

questions: what is a host identity tag
subtitle: An architecture that names computers by a public key instead of by where they are plugged in.

tldr.problem: IP addresses are used both as the name of a host and as its location, so a host that moves, sits behind a NAT or changes networks is hard to reach and hard to authenticate.
tldr.mechanism: The Host Identity namespace uses a public key as the name of a host. A Host Identity Protocol layer between the internetworking and transport layers binds transport associations to those identities and uses IP addresses only as locators.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9063 is an informational architecture memo that obsoletes RFC 4423. It also admits that HIP has not been a wild success in the Internet.

today: RFC 9063 is an Informational RFC published in July 2021 that obsoletes RFC 4423, and no later RFC obsoletes it. It states that HIP has been deployed in some settings but has not been a wild success in the Internet.

sections.title: Why a Host Identity Namespace
sections.content:
The Internet has two global namespaces: IP addresses and DNS names. RFC 9063 argues that we ask too much of them, and that a third namespace, the Host Identity namespace, fills a gap between the two. A Host Identity refers to a computing platform, and one platform may have several of them.

The architecture centres on Host Identifiers (HI) that are cryptographic: the HI is the public key of an asymmetric key pair. An identity is the abstract entity, and an identifier is the concrete bit pattern used to identify it. Payload traffic between two HIP hosts is typically, but not necessarily, protected with ESP, and the Host Identities are used to create the ESP security associations and to authenticate the hosts.

This document obsoletes RFC 4423. It widens the idea of Host Identities beyond IP connectivity to general secure signaling between hosts at any protocol layer.
sections.eli5: Computers today are only known by their address, like a house number. HIP adds a name tag made from a secret-based key, so a computer can prove who it is no matter where it is.

sections.title: Host Identifiers, HITs and LSIs
sections.content:
The Host Identifier is a public key, so it can be self-managed and is computationally difficult to forge. The HIP documents do not specify any other kind of identifier. The public key is never used directly at the transport or network layers. Two shorter forms stand in for it.

  • The Host Identity Tag (HIT) is a 128-bit hash over the public key, created from a Host Identity Hash, an IPv6 prefix and a hash identifier. It fits where an IPv6 address would go in the sockets API.
  • The Local Scope Identifier (LSI) is a 32-bit local representation that fits where an IPv4 address would go. LSIs are never transmitted on the wire. The HIP layer translates them to HITs and back.

Public Host Identifiers should be stored in DNS, using a new resource record type defined in RFC 8005. Unpublished identifiers should not be stored anywhere except on the communicating hosts. Through HIPv2 (RFC 7401), second preimage resistance of a HIT is 96 bits, less than the 128-bit width of an IPv6 address field because of the ORCHID prefix.
sections.eli5: The long secret-based name is too big to write everywhere, so HIP makes short nicknames from it. One nickname looks like a long address, and one looks like a short address, so old programs do not notice the change.

sections.title: A New Place in the Stack
sections.content:
Today an IP address plays two roles at once: it is the locator (where the host is in the topology) and the endpoint name. In the HIP architecture these are split. IP addresses stay locators, and Host Identifiers become the endpoint identifiers. A Host Identity can be reachable through several interfaces at the same time.

Transport associations such as TCP connections and UDP associations are no longer bound to IP addresses but to Host Identities, exposed as LSIs and HITs for legacy applications. The HIP layer is logically at Layer 3.5, between the transport and network layers. It acts as a shim for transport data that uses LSIs or HITs, and translates between them and routable IPv4 or IPv6 addresses.

A host may hold several identities, for example one published in DNS and one unpublished and rotated often for anonymous use. The RFC advises a unique identity per host, because copying an identity to many hosts means one compromise taints them all.
sections.eli5: Think of a pen pal who keeps moving. Letters go to their name, and a helper looks up the current street each time. The name stays, and only the street changes.

sections.title: Control Plane and Data Plane
sections.content:
HIP separates the control plane from the data plane. Two hosts start the control plane with the base exchange, a four-message key exchange that authenticates the Initiator and the Responder to each other using their public keys. It also creates symmetric keys, protected with HMACs, and includes a computational puzzle whose difficulty the Responder chooses, which lets the Responder stay stateless until the end of the exchange. Closing takes two messages.

After the exchange, the HIP layer keeps connections going when addresses change, using mobility (RFC 8046) and multihoming (RFC 8047) extensions. A moving host sends a HIP UPDATE packet with its new addresses, and the peer verifies reachability. To contact a mobile node, HIP offers a rendezvous mechanism (RFC 8004) and a relay mechanism (RFC 9028), which suits IPv4 networks with NATs.

For data, the most widely implemented option is ESP (RFC 7402). HITs appear in all control packets but not in ESP data packets, where the Security Parameter Index acts as a compressed HIT. For checksums, TCP and UDP use HITs in place of IP addresses in the pseudo header, and only the IPv6 pseudo header format is used.
sections.eli5: Two friends first swap secret handshakes, then talk in a private code. If one moves, they quickly check the new address is really them before carrying on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base exchange is built to resist resource exhaustion: the Responder starts the authenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange, its first packet can be prebuilt, and the puzzle can delay an Initiator when the Responder is overloaded. Man-in-the-middle attacks are hard to stop without third-party authentication. If the Responder's HI comes from a signed DNS zone or another secure source, the Initiator can authenticate the signed HIP packets. An Initiator using an unpublished HI knowingly risks such an attack.

Blindly accepting a new address would allow flooding attacks on third parties, so the mobility extensions include a return routability check before using an address for larger amounts of traffic. HITs can be used in access control lists, with the drawback that revoking a key may mean finding every list that holds it. The RFC also discusses opportunistic mode, in which the Initiator learns the Responder's identity during the exchange. This trades authentication for easier deployment and is framed with the four Trust On First Use principles of RFC 7435.
sections.eli5: Before sending a lot of mail to a new address, you ring the doorbell to check someone is really there. That stops a trickster from sending a flood of mail to a stranger's house.

sections.title: Benefits, Drawbacks and Adoption
sections.content:
The appendix lists benefits: applications stay unaware of address changes during handoffs, hosts in private address realms can still be told apart, IPv4 and IPv6 applications can interoperate through LSIs and HITs, and HIT-based access rules stay static as topology changes.

It also lists costs: a new layer and namespace need effort to implement and manage, a mapping is needed between HITs and locators, and the key exchange adds extra latency of two round trips. The most CPU-intensive steps are the asymmetric operations, which occur only during the key exchange, maintenance and teardown.

On adoption the RFC is candid. HIP has been deployed in an industrial control network in a production factory, but it has not been a wild success in the Internet, based on interviews with 19 experts cited from Levä et al. Demand was low and substitute technologies were favored.
sections.eli5: A name tag that follows you around is handy, but wearing one takes some effort and not everyone has picked it up yet.

layers.label: Application
layers.detail: Uses HITs or LSIs as if they were addresses

layers.label: Transport
layers.detail: TCP and UDP associations bound to Host Identities

layers.label: HIP layer (Layer 3.5)
layers.detail: Translates HITs and LSIs to routable IP addresses

layers.label: Network
layers.detail: IPv4 or IPv6 addresses act as locators
